questions.question: What is Big-O notation? Compare O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2^n) with Java examples.
questions.title: Big-O Notation — The Complexity Classes Every Java Developer Must Know
questions.direct_answer: **Big-O notation** describes the **asymptotic upper bound** on the growth rate of an algorithm's running time (or memory) as input size `n` grows to infinity. It expresses **how the cost scales with input**, not the absolute time. We drop constants and lower-order terms — O(3n + 5) becomes O(n), O(n² + n) becomes O(n²) — because they don't matter as n gets large. **The six complexity classes you need to know for interviews**: **O(1)** constant — hash map lookup (`HashMap.get`); **O(log n)** logarithmic — binary search, `TreeMap.get`, balanced BST operations; **O(n)** linear — list traversal, `ArrayList.contains`, summing an array; **O(n log n)** linearithmic — efficient sorts (merge sort, `Arrays.sort` for objects, `Collections.sort`); **O(n²)** quadratic — nested loops over the same input (naive bubble sort, pairwise comparison); **O(2^n)** exponential — naive recursive Fibonacci, subset enumeration, brute-force TSP. Two related notations: **Ω (big-Omega)** for **lower bound** (“at least this slow”), **Θ (big-Theta)** for **tight bound** (both upper and lower) — but in practice, interviewers say “O” and usually mean Θ. **Best / average / worst case** matter: `HashMap.get` is O(1) average but O(n) worst case (hash collisions chain to a list, or to a tree for Java 8+). Big-O tells you **how it scales**; actual wall-clock time depends on constant factors, cache locality, and branch prediction — sometimes an O(n²) algorithm beats O(n log n) for small `n` (e.g., insertion sort on tiny arrays). The interview win: **know the six classes, map each Java collection operation to one, and distinguish average vs worst case** for HashMap/HashSet/TreeMap.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can name and rank the common complexity classes, give Java examples of each, distinguish O from Ω/Θ, and understand best/average/worst case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing O(log n) with O(n log n). Saying HashMap.get() is always O(1) (it's O(1) *average*, O(n) worst case). Not dropping constants (calling it O(2n) instead of O(n))
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention amortized analysis, Java 8 HashMap's treeification at 8 entries per bucket (changing worst case to O(log n)), constant-factor reality (cache locality, branch prediction), and when O(n²) beats O(n log n) for small n

sections.title: What Big-O Actually Measures
sections.content:
Big-O describes **how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows** — not the absolute time. It's an asymptotic upper bound: 'this algorithm is **at most** this slow as n gets large.'

**Rules when deriving Big-O**:
1. **Drop constants**: `O(3n)` → `O(n)`; `O(500)` → `O(1)`.
2. **Drop non-dominant terms**: `O(n² + n)` → `O(n²)`; `O(n + log n)` → `O(n)`.
3. **Different inputs use different variables**: iterating two independent arrays is `O(a + b)`, not `O(n)`.
4. **Compound operations multiply**: nested loops over the same collection are `O(n²)`; loop with inner binary search is `O(n log n)`.

**Related notations**:
- **O (big-O)** — upper bound. 'At most this fast of growth.'
- **Ω (big-Omega)** — lower bound. 'At least this fast of growth.'
- **Θ (big-Theta)** — tight bound. Both O and Ω.
- Interview usage: people say 'O(n log n)' usually meaning **Θ(n log n)**.

**Best / average / worst case** — Big-O applies to any of these:
- `HashMap.get` — **best/average**: O(1); **worst**: O(log n) since Java 8 (was O(n) prior).
- QuickSort — **best/average**: O(n log n); **worst**: O(n²) (pathological pivot).
- Linear search — **best**: O(1) (target at position 0); **worst**: O(n); **average**: O(n/2) = O(n).

sections.title: The Six Classes — Growth at a Glance
sections.content:
| Class | Name | Example Java Operation | n=10 | n=1k | n=1M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **O(1)** | Constant | `HashMap.get`, array index | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| **O(log n)** | Logarithmic | Binary search, `TreeMap.get` | 3 | 10 | 20 |
| **O(n)** | Linear | `ArrayList.contains`, sum | 10 | 1,000 | 1,000,000 |
| **O(n log n)** | Linearithmic | `Collections.sort`, merge sort | 33 | 10,000 | 20,000,000 |
| **O(n²)** | Quadratic | Nested loops, bubble sort | 100 | 1,000,000 | 10^12 |
| **O(2^n)** | Exponential | Naive Fibonacci, subset gen | 1,024 | 10^301 | ∞ |

**Observations**:
- **Constants disappear**: at n=1M, O(n) = 1M operations regardless of whether we wrote O(n) or O(5n).
- **O(log n) is astonishingly cheap**: doubling n adds one step.
- **O(n²) becomes painful quickly**: n=1M means 10^12 ops — hours on a modern CPU.
- **O(2^n) is unusable beyond n≈30**: doubling n squares the cost.

sections.title: Java Examples of Each Class
Best / Average / Worst Case — Why It Matters
sections.content:
Big-O can describe any of these. For interviews, know both **average** and **worst** case for each operation.

**`HashMap` operations**:
- Average: **O(1)** — hash distributes entries evenly across buckets.
- Worst case (pre-Java 8): **O(n)** — all entries hash to same bucket; linear chain.
- Worst case (Java 8+): **O(log n)** — when a bucket exceeds 8 entries, the linked list is **treeified** into a red-black tree.
- **Amortized cost for put**: O(1) accounting for occasional resize.

**`ArrayList.add(x)`** (append at end):
- Average / best: **O(1)**.
- Worst case (single operation): **O(n)** — when capacity is exceeded, array doubles and all elements are copied.
- **Amortized**: **O(1)** — resize costs are spread across many adds.

**`ArrayList.add(0, x)`** (insert at front): always **O(n)** — shift all existing elements.

**QuickSort**:
- Best/average: **O(n log n)**.
- Worst case: **O(n²)** with a pathological pivot (sorted input with naive first-element pivot).
- Java's `Arrays.sort` uses **dual-pivot quicksort** for primitives, with O(n²) worst case but extremely rare in practice.

**Binary search**:
- Best: **O(1)** (target at mid on first check).
- Average/worst: **O(log n)**.

**TreeMap operations**: always **O(log n)** — red-black tree balances automatically, no degenerate case.

**Pro tip**: when someone says 'HashMap is O(1),' they mean average. If worst case matters (e.g., you can't trust input), `TreeMap` at O(log n) guaranteed is safer than `HashMap` at O(n) potential.

sections.title: Computing Big-O from Code
When Big-O Doesn't Match Real Performance
sections.content:
Big-O is a **theoretical tool**. Real-world performance depends on:

**1. Constants** — O(n) with low constant can beat O(log n) for small n.
- Example: linear scan of 10 elements faster than binary search of 10 elements (setup cost).
- Java `Arrays.sort` uses **insertion sort** for arrays under ~47 elements — O(n²) but fast for small n.

**2. Cache locality** — sequential access beats random access.
- `ArrayList` traversal (contiguous memory) far faster than `LinkedList` (pointer-chasing) despite both being O(n).
- Reason: CPU cache lines, prefetching, branch prediction.

**3. Branch prediction** — predictable branches are nearly free; unpredictable ones cost 10-20 cycles.

**4. Memory allocation** — `new` is O(1) but expensive in absolute terms; avoid in hot loops.

**5. JIT optimization** — Java's JIT optimizes hot paths aggressively; Big-O estimates don't reflect JIT wins.

**Example — insertion sort vs merge sort**:
- Merge sort: O(n log n) — better asymptotically.
- Insertion sort: O(n²) — worse asymptotically.
- **For n < 50, insertion sort wins** — less overhead per element.
- Java's Timsort and `Arrays.sort` exploit this: use insertion sort on small sub-ranges.

**Takeaway**: **Big-O is necessary but not sufficient**. For hot code paths, benchmark. For typical 'choose the right data structure' decisions, Big-O is your guide.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Big-O** describes asymptotic growth of running time (or memory) as n → ∞.
- **Drop constants** (O(3n) → O(n)) and **non-dominant terms** (O(n² + n) → O(n²)).
- **Six classes to know**: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2^n).
- **O(1)**: hash lookup, array index.
- **O(log n)**: binary search, TreeMap ops.
- **O(n)**: list traversal, ArrayList.contains.
- **O(n log n)**: Collections.sort, merge sort, Arrays.sort for objects.
- **O(n²)**: nested loops over same input, bubble sort, naive pairwise.
- **O(2^n)**: naive recursive Fibonacci, subset enumeration.
- **O / Ω / Θ**: upper / lower / tight bounds. Interview 'O' usually means Θ.
- **Best / average / worst** matter: HashMap is O(1) avg, O(log n) worst (Java 8+).
- **Amortized cost** — ArrayList.add and HashMap.put are O(1) amortized (occasional resize).
- **Real performance ≠ Big-O**: cache locality, constants, JIT all matter.
- **For small n, O(n²) may beat O(n log n)** — Timsort uses insertion sort on small ranges.
- **Common trap**: O(n) operation (contains, get by value) inside O(n) loop → O(n²). Fix with HashMap/HashSet.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Big-O notation** describes the asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's running time (or memory) scales with input size. We drop constants and lower-order terms because they don't matter as n gets large.

**The six classes you need to know**

**O(1) — constant**
- Independent of input size
- HashMap.get, HashSet.contains, array index, ArrayDeque.offer
- 1 step whether n is 10 or 10 million

**O(log n) — logarithmic**
- Each step halves the remaining work
- Binary search, TreeMap.get, PriorityQueue.poll
- 20 steps for n=1M

**O(n) — linear**
- Work proportional to input size
- ArrayList.contains, summing an array, list traversal

**O(n log n) — linearithmic**
- Collections.sort, Arrays.sort for objects, merge sort, Timsort
- Best achievable for comparison-based sorting

**O(n²) — quadratic**
- Nested loops over same input
- Bubble sort, naive pairwise comparison
- Becomes painful at n=1M (10^12 ops)

**O(2^n) — exponential**
- Naive recursive Fibonacci
- Subset enumeration
- Unusable beyond n≈30

**Related notations**
- O (big-O) — upper bound
- Ω (big-Omega) — lower bound
- Θ (big-Theta) — tight bound (both)
- Interview 'O' usually means Θ in practice

**Best / average / worst case**
- HashMap.get — O(1) average, O(log n) worst case since Java 8 (was O(n) prior due to linked list chains)
- QuickSort — O(n log n) average, O(n²) pathological
- Binary search — O(1) best, O(log n) average/worst
- TreeMap — always O(log n), no degenerate case

**Amortized cost**
- ArrayList.add is O(1) worst-case single op but O(n) occasional resize; amortized O(1)
- HashMap.put same story
- Amortization spreads the occasional O(n) across many O(1) ops

**Computing Big-O from code**
- Walk the code mentally, count operations as function of n
- Single loop: O(n)
- Nested loops same n: O(n²)
- Nested loops different vars: O(a·b)
- Loop with halving step: O(log n)
- Loop with inner binary search: O(n log n)
- Recursion that branches into 2: O(2^n)
- Divide and combine (merge sort): O(n log n) via master theorem

**Common traps**

**1. O(n) operation inside O(n) loop → O(n²)**
- `for (x : list) if (list.contains(y)) {...}` — contains is O(n), total O(n²)
- Fix: use HashSet — contains becomes O(1), total O(n)

**2. Saying HashMap.get() is O(1) always**
- It's O(1) average
- Worst case O(log n) since Java 8 (treeification at 8 entries per bucket)
- Worst case O(n) pre-Java 8

**3. Not dropping constants**
- O(3n) is O(n)
- O(500) is O(1)
- O(n + log n) is O(n)

**When Big-O doesn't match real performance**
- Constants matter: O(n) with low constant can beat O(log n) for small n
- Cache locality: ArrayList traversal beats LinkedList traversal (same Big-O)
- Branch prediction
- Memory allocation cost
- JIT optimization of hot paths
- For n < 50, insertion sort (O(n²)) beats merge sort (O(n log n)) — Timsort exploits this

**Takeaway**
- Big-O is necessary but not sufficient
- For algorithm choice: use Big-O
- For hot-path performance: benchmark
- For Java collections: know average AND worst case

**Recommendation:** For Java interviews, **memorize the six complexity classes** and **map each Java collection operation to one**. Know **HashMap is O(1) average, O(log n) worst case** (Java 8 treeification). Know **ArrayList.add is amortized O(1)** — resize is occasional. Know **Collections.sort is O(n log n)** — Timsort is stable and adaptive. Watch for the classic trap: **O(n) operation inside O(n) loop** (e.g., `list.contains` in a loop over `list`) — convert to HashMap/HashSet for O(n) total. Remember **Big-O measures growth, not speed** — constants and cache locality matter in practice, but for choosing between data structures, Big-O is your primary guide. When asked 'what's the complexity?' always specify **best/average/worst** for hash-based structures; give **amortized** for resize-based structures. Never say 'HashMap is always O(1)' — say 'O(1) average, O(log n) worst case since Java 8.' This demonstrates both depth and precision.

questions.question: What's the time complexity of get/add/remove/contains for ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, TreeMap, HashSet, LinkedHashMap, ArrayDeque, and PriorityQueue?
questions.title: Time Complexity of Java Collection Operations — The Cheat Sheet
questions.direct_answer: Memorize these five rows because they show up in every Java interview: **`ArrayList`** — `get(i)` **O(1)**, `add(e)` **amortized O(1)** (resize is occasional O(n)), `add(i, e)` / `remove(i)` **O(n)** (shift), `contains` **O(n)**. **`LinkedList`** — `get(i)` **O(n)** (must walk), `add(e)` / `addFirst` / `addLast` **O(1)**, `remove(first/last)` **O(1)**, `contains` **O(n)**; use it only when you need O(1) insertion at both ends (`ArrayDeque` is usually better). **`HashMap` / `HashSet` / `LinkedHashMap`** — `get`, `put`, `remove`, `contains` all **O(1) average** and **O(log n) worst case** (Java 8 treeifies buckets with 8+ entries). **`TreeMap` / `TreeSet`** — all ops **O(log n) guaranteed** (red-black tree); plus range operations (`subMap`, `headMap`, `firstKey`) same **O(log n)**. **`ArrayDeque`** — `offerFirst`/`offerLast`/`pollFirst`/`pollLast` all **O(1) amortized**; prefer over `LinkedList` and `Stack`. **`PriorityQueue`** — `offer` / `poll` **O(log n)**, `peek` **O(1)**, `contains` / `remove(element)` **O(n)** (linear scan). The decision rule: **random access by index** → ArrayList; **frequent insertion/removal in the middle** → LinkedList (rare); **key→value lookup** → HashMap (O(1) avg) or TreeMap (ordered, O(log n)); **set membership** → HashSet; **FIFO/LIFO** → ArrayDeque (never Stack); **always-smallest element** → PriorityQueue; **insertion-order iteration** → LinkedHashMap. Watch out for `LinkedList.get(i)` being O(n) (common trap) and `PriorityQueue.contains` being O(n) (not O(log n)!).

sections.title: The Complete Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
| Collection | Access | Insert (end) | Insert (middle) | Delete | Contains | Ordered? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ArrayList** | O(1) | amortized O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | insertion |
| **LinkedList** | O(n) | O(1) | O(n) to find + O(1) insert | O(1) if have node ref | O(n) | insertion |
| **ArrayDeque** | N/A | O(1) amortized | N/A | O(1) (first/last) | O(n) | insertion |
| **HashMap** | — | O(1) avg / O(log n) worst | — | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | none |
| **LinkedHashMap** | — | O(1) avg | — | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | insertion or access |
| **TreeMap** | — | O(log n) | — | O(log n) | O(log n) | sorted by key |
| **HashSet** | — | O(1) avg | — | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | none |
| **LinkedHashSet** | — | O(1) avg | — | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | insertion |
| **TreeSet** | — | O(log n) | — | O(log n) | O(log n) | sorted |
| **PriorityQueue** | peek O(1) | offer O(log n) | — | poll O(log n); remove(e) O(n) | O(n) | heap order |
| **Stack** (legacy) | O(1) peek | O(1) push | — | O(1) pop | O(n) | LIFO |
| **Vector** (legacy) | O(1) | O(1) amortized | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | insertion |

**Notation**: 'O(1) avg' means average case; worst case is listed separately where different.

sections.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList — The Classic Trap
sections.content:
**ArrayList is backed by a resizable array**. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list.

```java
ArrayList<Integer> al = new ArrayList<>();
al.get(500);       // O(1) — direct array index
al.add(42);        // amortized O(1) — append at end
al.add(0, 42);     // O(n) — shift all elements right
al.remove(500);    // O(n) — shift all subsequent elements left
al.contains(42);   // O(n) — linear scan

LinkedList<Integer> ll = new LinkedList<>();
ll.get(500);       // O(n) — walk 500 nodes!
ll.add(42);        // O(1) — append at tail
ll.addFirst(42);   // O(1) — prepend
ll.remove(500);    // O(n) — walk to find, then unlink
ll.contains(42);   // O(n)
```

**The surprising truth**: **`LinkedList` is almost always the wrong choice** in modern Java:
- Cache locality favors `ArrayList` even for insertions/removals (contiguous memory).
- `LinkedList.get(i)` is O(n) — you cannot index randomly.
- For queue/deque operations, `ArrayDeque` is faster than `LinkedList` (no pointer-chasing).
- The only case `LinkedList` wins: very frequent insertions at a known iterator position (`ListIterator.add`).

**Decision rule**:
- Need indexed access? → `ArrayList`.
- Need queue/deque (FIFO/LIFO)? → `ArrayDeque`.
- Need to insert at both ends frequently with no indexing? → `ArrayDeque` (still wins).

sections.title: HashMap, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap — Lookup Structures
sections.content:
**HashMap** — O(1) average, O(log n) worst case (Java 8+):
```java
HashMap<String, User> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("alice", user);   // O(1) average
map.get("alice");          // O(1) average
map.containsKey("alice");  // O(1) average
map.remove("alice");       // O(1) average
```
Java 8 treeifies a bucket into a red-black tree when it has 8+ entries — worst case becomes O(log n) instead of O(n).

**TreeMap** — guaranteed O(log n), sorted by key:
```java
TreeMap<String, User> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put("alice", user);    // O(log n)
map.firstKey();             // O(log n) — leftmost node
map.lastKey();              // O(log n)
map.subMap("a", "m");       // O(log n) — view, not copy
map.ceilingKey("b");        // O(log n) — smallest key ≥ 'b'
map.floorKey("b");          // O(log n) — largest key ≤ 'b'
```
Use when you need **ordered** iteration or **range queries**.

**LinkedHashMap** — O(1) average + preserves iteration order:
```java
LinkedHashMap<String, User> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
map.put("alice", user1);
map.put("bob",   user2);
// Iteration: alice, bob (insertion order)

// Access-order mode — useful for LRU caches
LinkedHashMap<K,V> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true);
// Iteration order shifts to most-recently-accessed last
```
Same O(1) performance as HashMap; small memory overhead for the doubly-linked list maintaining order.

**Decision**:
- Unordered fast lookup → `HashMap`.
- Sorted iteration or range queries → `TreeMap`.
- Insertion-order iteration (or access-order for LRU) → `LinkedHashMap`.

sections.title: ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue, Stack
sections.content:
**ArrayDeque** — the modern `Stack`/`Queue`/`Deque`:
```java
Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.offerFirst(1);   // O(1) amortized — push to front
dq.offerLast(2);    // O(1) amortized — push to back
dq.pollFirst();     // O(1) amortized — pop from front
dq.pollLast();      // O(1) amortized — pop from back
dq.peekFirst();     // O(1)
dq.contains(1);     // O(n) — linear scan
```
**Use `ArrayDeque` instead of `Stack`** — `Stack` is a legacy synchronized class extending `Vector`; it's slow and has a weird API. `Deque` interface offers `push()`/`pop()` too.

**PriorityQueue** — binary heap:
```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(5);       // O(log n) — sift up
pq.offer(2);       
pq.offer(8);       
pq.peek();         // O(1) — returns 2 (smallest)
pq.poll();         // O(log n) — returns 2, sifts root down
pq.contains(5);    // O(n) — NOT O(log n)!
pq.remove(5);      // O(n) — find + heap rebuild
```
Default is min-heap (natural order). For max-heap: `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())`.

**Common trap**: `pq.contains` and `pq.remove(element)` are **O(n)** — there's no hash index. If you need efficient contains on a priority queue, maintain a separate HashMap.

**Stack (legacy — don't use)**:
```java
Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>();   // legacy, synchronized, extends Vector
s.push(1);       // O(1) but synchronized (slow)
// Use ArrayDeque as Deque instead:
Deque<Integer> s2 = new ArrayDeque<>();
s2.push(1);
s2.pop();
```

sections.title: The Decision Matrix
sections.content:
**For indexed sequential data**:
- Random access by position → **ArrayList**.
- Only append/iterate → **ArrayList**.
- Frequent front/back ops, no indexing → **ArrayDeque** (not LinkedList).

**For key-value mapping**:
- Unordered, fast lookup → **HashMap**.
- Sorted by key, range queries → **TreeMap**.
- Insertion-order iteration → **LinkedHashMap**.
- LRU cache behavior → **LinkedHashMap** with access-order mode, or **Caffeine/Guava**.
- Thread-safe, high concurrency → **ConcurrentHashMap**.
- Enum keys → **EnumMap** (O(1) with no hash).

**For set membership**:
- Fast contains → **HashSet**.
- Sorted iteration → **TreeSet**.
- Insertion order → **LinkedHashSet**.
- Enum elements → **EnumSet** (bit set, very fast).

**For queue / stack / deque**:
- LIFO stack → **ArrayDeque** (`push`/`pop`).
- FIFO queue → **ArrayDeque** or **LinkedList** (ArrayDeque wins).

**Immutable snapshots** (Java 9+):
- `List.of(...)`, `Set.of(...)`, `Map.of(...)` — immutable, compact, fast.
- Throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on mutation.
- Throws NPE on null keys/values.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Memorize these five rows because they show up in every Java interview.

**ArrayList**
- get(i): O(1)
- add(e) append: amortized O(1) — occasional resize is O(n)
- add(i, e) middle: O(n) — shift
- remove(i): O(n) — shift
- contains: O(n) — linear scan

**LinkedList**
- get(i): O(n) — must walk; common trap
- addFirst / addLast: O(1)
- remove first / last: O(1)
- contains: O(n)
- Almost always wrong choice in modern Java
- ArrayDeque beats it for deque ops

**ArrayDeque** — modern Stack/Queue replacement
- offerFirst, offerLast, pollFirst, pollLast: O(1) amortized
- peekFirst, peekLast: O(1)
- contains: O(n)
- Use instead of Stack (legacy, synchronized, slow)

**HashMap / HashSet / LinkedHashMap**
- get, put, remove, contains: O(1) average
- Worst case: O(log n) since Java 8 (treeification at 8 entries per bucket)
- Worst case O(n) pre-Java 8

**TreeMap / TreeSet**
- All ops: O(log n) guaranteed (red-black tree)
- Range queries (subMap, headMap, ceilingKey, floorKey): O(log n)
- Use for sorted iteration or range queries

**LinkedHashMap**
- Same O(1) as HashMap
- Preserves insertion order (default) OR access-order (useful for LRU cache)
- Small memory overhead for linked list

**PriorityQueue** (binary heap)
- offer: O(log n) — sift up
- poll: O(log n) — sift down
- peek: O(1)
- contains: O(n) — NOT O(log n); common trap
- remove(element): O(n)
- Default min-heap; for max-heap use Comparator.reverseOrder()

**Legacy — don't use**
- Stack: synchronized, slow; use ArrayDeque
- Vector: synchronized, slow; use ArrayList
- Hashtable: synchronized; use ConcurrentHashMap

**Common traps**

**1. LinkedList.get(i) is O(n)**
- Must walk the links
- Never use LinkedList for indexed access

**2. PriorityQueue.contains is O(n)**
- No hash index
- If you need efficient contains, maintain a separate HashMap

**3. ArrayList.add(0, e) is O(n)**
- Shifts everything right
- Use ArrayDeque if you need front-insertion

**4. HashMap.get() is not always O(1)**
- O(1) average, O(log n) worst case
- Depends on hash distribution and treeification

**5. ArrayList.remove(i) is O(n)**
- Shifts all subsequent elements left

**Decision matrix**

**Indexed sequential data**
- Random access → ArrayList
- Front/back ops → ArrayDeque

**Key→value lookup**
- Unordered fast → HashMap
- Sorted / range → TreeMap
- Insertion/access order → LinkedHashMap
- Thread-safe → ConcurrentHashMap
- Enum keys → EnumMap

**Set membership**
- Fast contains → HashSet
- Sorted iteration → TreeSet
- Insertion order → LinkedHashSet
- Enum elements → EnumSet (bitset, very fast)

**Stack / Queue / Deque**
- LIFO stack → ArrayDeque (push/pop)
- FIFO queue → ArrayDeque
- Priority → PriorityQueue
- Concurrent queue → ConcurrentLinkedDeque, LinkedBlockingQueue

**Immutable snapshots (Java 9+)**
- List.of, Set.of, Map.of
- Compact, fast, throw on mutation, throw NPE on null

**Amortized O(1)**
- ArrayList.add and HashMap.put
- Single op can be O(n) (resize)
- Over many ops, averages to O(1)
- Spread the occasional big cost across many small ones

**Recommendation:** Memorize the table — this is the most common Java interview question category. For **each operation**, know both **average and worst case** for hash-based structures, and **amortized** for resize-based. The big decisions: **`ArrayList` for indexed**, **`ArrayDeque` for stack/queue/deque**, **`HashMap` for O(1) lookup**, **`TreeMap` for sorted/range**, **`LinkedHashMap` for insertion-order or LRU**, **`PriorityQueue` for always-smallest**. Avoid **`LinkedList`** in modern code — `ArrayDeque` wins for deque ops, `ArrayList` for indexed. Avoid **`Stack`**, **`Vector`**, **`Hashtable`** — legacy synchronized; use the modern non-synchronized versions. Remember the three classic traps: **`LinkedList.get(i)` is O(n)**, **`PriorityQueue.contains` is O(n) (not log n)**, **`ArrayList.add(0, e)` is O(n)**. In interviews, always qualify hash structures: 'O(1) average, O(log n) worst case since Java 8' — shows depth and precision.

questions.question: What is amortized complexity? Why is `ArrayList.add()` amortized O(1) when a single add can be O(n)?
questions.title: Amortized Complexity — Why ArrayList.add and HashMap.put Are Really O(1)
questions.direct_answer: **Amortized complexity** is the **average cost per operation over a long sequence**, accounting for occasional expensive operations spread across many cheap ones. A single `ArrayList.add(e)` can be **O(1)** (just drop the value into the next array slot) **or O(n)** (when capacity is exceeded, allocate a bigger array and copy all existing elements). The worst-case single operation is O(n) — but it's so rare that, **averaged across all adds, the cost per add is O(1)**. This is called **amortized O(1)**. Proof by aggregate analysis: `ArrayList` doubles capacity when full (default growth factor 1.5x in Java, but doubling is easier to analyze). For n adds starting from capacity 1, total resize work is `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 = n - 1` element copies plus n inserts — total 2n − 1 ops = O(n), divided by n adds = **O(1) per add**. Same pattern for **`HashMap.put`**: when load factor exceeds 0.75, the internal table doubles and every entry is rehashed into the new table — one put can be O(n) — but the cost averages to **O(1) per put**. **Why it matters**: you can treat `list.add()` and `map.put()` as cheap in algorithm analysis, even knowing individual ops can occasionally block. **The trade-off**: amortized bounds hide worst-case latency; if you need **predictable per-op latency** (real-time systems, low-latency trading), amortized O(1) isn't good enough — pre-size the collection (`new ArrayList<>(knownCapacity)`) to avoid resize. Three amortization techniques exist: **aggregate** (total cost / n), **accounting method** (charge extra 'credit' to cheap ops to pay for expensive ones), and **potential method** (formal analysis via a potential function). For interviews, the aggregate argument is usually enough.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands amortized analysis (not just 'average case'), can prove ArrayList.add is amortized O(1) via the doubling argument, and knows when amortization isn't good enough
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing amortized with average-case (they're different concepts). Not knowing why doubling (vs adding a fixed amount) gives O(1) amortized. Claiming a single ArrayList.add is always O(1)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the aggregate analysis proof, mention the three techniques (aggregate / accounting / potential method), discuss why low-latency systems avoid amortization, and reference Java's actual 1.5x growth factor

sections.title: Amortized vs Worst-Case vs Average-Case
sections.content:
Three distinct concepts that get conflated:

**Worst-case complexity**: the maximum cost of a **single operation**. For `ArrayList.add`, worst case is **O(n)** (when resize happens).

**Average-case complexity**: the expected cost of a single operation, over some input distribution. For `HashMap.get`, average case (with good hash distribution) is **O(1)**.

**Amortized complexity**: the **average cost per operation across a sequence of n operations**, in the worst case of input sequences. It's a **guarantee**, not a probabilistic statement. For `ArrayList.add`, **amortized O(1)** means: n adds cost O(n) total — always, no matter the input.

**The key difference from average-case**:
- Average-case assumes a probability distribution over inputs.
- Amortized is worst-case **across the whole sequence**, no distribution assumed.
- A single amortized-O(1) operation can still be O(n), but you're guaranteed the total over n ops is O(n).

**Why amortized is useful**:
- Simpler reasoning: 'treat add as O(1)' is easier than tracking resize timing.
- Tight bounds: an algorithm that does n `list.add`s is O(n) total — the amortized bound gives you the right total cost.

**When amortized is NOT enough**:
- Real-time systems (robotics, avionics, trading) care about worst-case per-op, not averages.
- For those, pre-size collections to avoid resize: `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)`.

sections.title: ArrayList.add — The Doubling Argument
sections.content:
**How Java's ArrayList grows**:
```java
// Simplified ArrayList internals
Object[] elements;    // backing array
int size;             // number of elements currently

public void add(E e) {
    if (size == elements.length) {
        // CAPACITY FULL — grow the array
        int newCapacity = elements.length * 3 / 2 + 1;  // ~1.5x
        Object[] newArr = new Object[newCapacity];
        System.arraycopy(elements, 0, newArr, 0, size);  // O(n) copy
        elements = newArr;
    }
    elements[size++] = e;   // O(1) insert
}
```

**Single-op worst case**: O(n) when resize happens.
**Amortized proof** (using doubling for simplicity; Java uses 1.5x but the argument is the same):

Starting from capacity 1, after n adds, resizes happen at sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., up to n/2.

Total resize cost (element copies): `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 ≈ n`.
Total insert cost: `n` (one per add).
**Total cost over n adds**: `~2n = O(n)`.
**Amortized cost per add**: `O(n) / n = O(1)`.

**Why doubling works**: each resize doubles the capacity, so resizes become exponentially rarer. The total copy work is bounded by a geometric series (1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 < 2n).

**Why adding a fixed increment (say, +10) does NOT work**:
- Capacity: 10, 20, 30, 40, ...
- Resizes happen every 10 adds.
- Total copy work: `10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n = n(n/10)/2 = O(n²)`.
- Amortized per add: O(n), not O(1).

That's why all growing-array data structures (`ArrayList`, `StringBuilder`, Go slices, Python lists, C++ vectors) use **multiplicative growth** — usually 1.5x or 2x.

**Avoiding amortization**:
```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(expectedSize);   // pre-size
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) list.add(i);              // no resize — always O(1)
```

sections.title: HashMap.put — Same Story with Rehash
The Three Techniques of Amortized Analysis
sections.content:
Formal amortized analysis has three standard approaches — interviewers rarely ask but knowing them marks you as advanced.

**1. Aggregate analysis** (simplest):
- Compute the total cost of n operations: T(n).
- Amortized cost per op = T(n) / n.
- Works for `ArrayList.add`: T(n) = 2n – 1 → amortized O(1).

**2. Accounting method** (also called 'banker's method'):
- Charge each operation more than its actual cost.
- Extra 'credit' is stored and used to pay for expensive ops.
- For ArrayList.add: charge 3 per add (1 for insert + 2 for future resize).
  - When capacity doubles from k to 2k, we've added k elements since the last resize, each contributing 2 credit = 2k credit — enough to cover the k-element copy.
- Amortized cost: 3 = O(1) per op.

**3. Potential method** (most formal):
- Define a potential function Φ over the data structure's state.
- Amortized cost of op i = actual cost + ΔΦ.
- For ArrayList: Φ = 2 × (size – capacity / 2).
  - When inserting into a non-full array: actual cost 1, ΔΦ = 2, amortized = 3.
  - When resizing from cap k to 2k: actual cost k + 1, ΔΦ = –(2k – 2) + 2 = –2k + 4, amortized = k + 1 – 2k + 4 = 5 – k, but bounded by 3 via careful Φ choice.
- The potential 'stores' work for future expensive ops.

**Which to use?**
- Aggregate: simplest; use for exam-style proofs.
- Accounting: intuitive; use to communicate the 'prepaid credit' idea.
- Potential: most formal; use for research papers or complex data structures.

For interviews, **aggregate** is sufficient: 'n adds cost 2n total — so O(1) amortized per add.'

sections.title: When Amortized Bounds Are Not Enough
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Amortized complexity** = average cost per operation across a sequence, worst-case guarantee.
- **Different from average-case** (average-case assumes probability distribution; amortized doesn't).
- **Different from worst-case** (a single op can exceed the amortized bound; the total is bounded).
- **ArrayList.add** is amortized O(1) despite worst-case single O(n) (resize).
- **HashMap.put** is amortized O(1) despite worst-case single O(n) (rehash).
- **Doubling capacity** gives O(1) amortized; fixed-size increments give O(n) amortized.
- **Aggregate analysis**: n adds cost 2n total → amortized O(1).
- **Three formal techniques**: aggregate, accounting (banker's), potential method.
- **Pre-sizing** avoids resize: `new ArrayList<>(n)` or `new HashMap<>(expectedSize)`.
- **Java's growth factors**: ArrayList 1.5x (3/2 + 1), HashMap 2x.
- **HashMap load factor** 0.75 default; resize when size ≥ capacity × 0.75.
- **Real-time / low-latency** systems need worst-case bounds — pre-size or use bounded structures.
- **Concurrent** — amortized bounds assume single-thread; ConcurrentHashMap uses different strategies.
- **Memory trade-off**: amortization wastes ~25% space on average; `trimToSize` to reclaim.
- **Interview tip**: say 'amortized O(1)' explicitly — not just 'O(1)' — shows depth.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Amortized complexity** is the **average cost per operation over a long sequence**, accounting for occasional expensive operations spread across many cheap ones.

**ArrayList.add — the canonical example**
- Single `add(e)`: usually O(1) (drop value into next array slot)
- When capacity is exceeded: O(n) (allocate bigger array, copy all elements)
- Worst-case single op: O(n)
- But amortized across all adds: O(1)

**Why? The doubling argument**
- ArrayList grows ~1.5x when full (Java default)
- For simpler math, assume doubling
- Starting from capacity 1, after n adds, resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., n/2
- Total resize cost: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 ≈ n element copies
- Total insert cost: n
- Total over n adds: ~2n = O(n)
- Amortized per add: O(n) / n = O(1)

**Why doubling, not fixed increments?**
- If we grew by +10 each time: resizes at 10, 20, 30, ...
- Total copy work: 10 + 20 + ... + n = O(n²)
- Amortized: O(n) per add — bad
- Multiplicative growth (1.5x, 2x) is essential for O(1) amortized
- All resizable arrays use this: Java ArrayList, Go slices, Python lists, C++ vectors

**HashMap.put — same story**
- When size ≥ capacity × load factor (0.75 default), rehash
- One put: O(1) normal, O(n) during resize
- Amortized: O(1)

**Amortized vs average-case vs worst-case**

**Worst-case**: max cost of a single operation
- ArrayList.add: O(n)

**Average-case**: expected cost over probability distribution of inputs
- HashMap.get: O(1) with good hash

**Amortized**: average per op over a sequence, worst-case guarantee
- ArrayList.add over n ops: total O(n) ALWAYS, no matter input

Key difference: amortized is a guarantee; average-case is probabilistic.

**Three formal techniques**

**1. Aggregate analysis** (simplest, interview-friendly)
- Total cost of n ops: T(n)
- Amortized per op: T(n) / n
- ArrayList: T(n) = 2n → O(1) amortized

**2. Accounting method (banker's)**
- Charge each op more than actual cost
- Extra credit prepays for expensive ops
- For ArrayList: charge 3 per add — enough to cover future resize

**3. Potential method**
- Define a potential function Φ over the data structure state
- Amortized cost = actual cost + ΔΦ
- Most formal, used in research

For interviews: aggregate is sufficient.

**When amortized is not enough**

**Real-time systems**
- Trading, avionics, robotics
- p99/p999 latency SLAs can't tolerate occasional O(n) blips
- Solution: pre-size to avoid resize
- `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)` or `new HashMap<>((int)(n / 0.75f) + 1)`

**Concurrent systems**
- Amortized bounds assume single-thread
- ConcurrentHashMap uses incremental resize to avoid blocking
- Segment-based (Java 7) or fully concurrent (Java 8+)

**Memory-constrained systems**
- 1.5x growth wastes ~25% space on average
- Use `ArrayList.trimToSize()` to reclaim
- Or use fixed-size arrays if size is known

**Pre-sizing to avoid amortization**

```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(expectedSize);
for (int i = 0; i < expectedSize; i++) list.add(i);
// No resize — every add is O(1) worst case
```

**Key takeaways**

**1. Treat ArrayList.add and HashMap.put as O(1)** in algorithm analysis

**2. Know that a single op can be O(n)** under resize

**3. Pre-size when you know the size** — especially for hot paths and large batches

**4. Say 'amortized O(1)' explicitly** — not just 'O(1)' — shows depth in interviews

**5. Amortization hides worst-case latency** — real-time systems need different strategies

**Recommendation:** In interviews, when asked about `ArrayList.add` or `HashMap.put`, say **'amortized O(1)'** explicitly — not just 'O(1).' Explain with the **doubling argument**: 'n adds cost 2n total element copies because each resize doubles the capacity, so resizes are exponentially rarer. The geometric sum `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2` is bounded by n.' Distinguish **amortized from average-case**: amortized is a worst-case guarantee over a sequence; average-case assumes a probability distribution. For **production code**: **pre-size collections** when the size is knowable (`new ArrayList<>(n)`, `new HashMap<>((int)(n / 0.75f) + 1)`) — this eliminates resize entirely and gives you true per-op O(1). For **real-time / low-latency systems**, amortized isn't good enough; use **pre-sized or bounded collections**, profile p99 latency, and consider `ConcurrentHashMap` which uses incremental resize. For **interviews at trading or systems firms**, knowing the three techniques (aggregate, accounting, potential method) marks you as advanced — though aggregate is usually sufficient. The mental model: **amortization spreads occasional big costs across many small ones**; it's a mathematical accounting trick that lets us reason about collections as if they're always cheap, while the implementation quietly handles the occasional expensive moment.

questions.question: How do you analyze the time complexity of a recursive algorithm? Cover the master theorem, recursion tree, and Fibonacci / merge sort / binary search examples.
questions.title: Analyzing Recursive Algorithm Complexity — Master Theorem, Recursion Tree, Substitution
questions.direct_answer: To analyze a recursive algorithm, **write a recurrence relation** that expresses its running time on input size n in terms of its running time on smaller sub-problems, then **solve the recurrence**. Three standard techniques: **(1) Substitution method** — guess a bound, prove it by induction (used when you already suspect the answer). **(2) Recursion tree** — draw the tree of recursive calls, compute the work at each level, sum up (intuitive and works for most practical cases). **(3) Master theorem** — a formula that solves recurrences of the form **T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)**, where `a` is the number of sub-problems and `n/b` is each sub-problem's size. The three master-theorem cases: **Case 1** — if `f(n) = O(n^(log_b(a) − ε))`, then T(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a)) (the leaves dominate). **Case 2** — if `f(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a))`, then T(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a) · log n) (balanced). **Case 3** — if `f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b(a) + ε))` with regularity, then T(n) = Θ(f(n)) (the root work dominates). **Examples**: **Merge sort** `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)` — a=2, b=2, log_b(a) = 1, f(n) = n = Θ(n^1) → Case 2 → **Θ(n log n)**. **Binary search** `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)` — a=1, b=2, log_b(a) = 0, f(n) = 1 = Θ(n^0) → Case 2 → **Θ(log n)**. **Naive Fibonacci** `T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)` — NOT a master-theorem form (doesn't divide into equal sub-problems); use recursion tree to see branching factor ≈2 per level, depth n → **O(2^n)** (more precisely O(φ^n) where φ ≈ 1.618). Key intuition: **fewer sub-problems or smaller size = cheaper**; **more or bigger = more expensive**. Memoization or iteration converts exponential recursion to polynomial.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write a recurrence from code, solve it with the master theorem OR recursion tree, and recognize common patterns (merge sort, binary search, Fibonacci)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to apply master theorem to non-master-form recurrences (like Fibonacci). Forgetting to identify f(n). Confusing the base of the log in master theorem
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Know all three master-theorem cases with examples, explain recursion tree intuitively, mention that Fibonacci with memoization is O(n), reference T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) as 'the merge sort recurrence'

sections.title: From Code to Recurrence
Master Theorem — Plug-and-Play for Most Cases
sections.content:
**Form**: `T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)` where `a ≥ 1`, `b > 1`, `f(n)` is asymptotically positive.

**Compute the critical exponent**: `c = log_b(a)`.

**Three cases**:

**Case 1 — leaves dominate**:
- If `f(n) = O(n^(c − ε))` for some ε > 0, then **T(n) = Θ(n^c)**.
- Intuition: non-recursive work is smaller than the number of leaves; leaves swamp the total.

**Case 2 — balanced**:
- If `f(n) = Θ(n^c)`, then **T(n) = Θ(n^c · log n)**.
- Intuition: work at each level is the same; depth is log n.

**Case 3 — root dominates**:
- If `f(n) = Ω(n^(c + ε))` for some ε > 0, AND `a · f(n/b) ≤ k · f(n)` for some k < 1 (regularity), then **T(n) = Θ(f(n))**.
- Intuition: non-recursive work at the root dominates.

**Worked examples**:

**Merge sort**: `T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n)`
- a=2, b=2, c = log_2(2) = 1
- f(n) = n = Θ(n^1) = Θ(n^c)
- Case 2 → **T(n) = Θ(n log n)**.

**Binary search**: `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`
- a=1, b=2, c = log_2(1) = 0
- f(n) = 1 = Θ(n^0) = Θ(n^c)
- Case 2 → **T(n) = Θ(log n)**.

**Strassen's matrix multiply**: `T(n) = 7 T(n/2) + O(n²)`
- a=7, b=2, c = log_2(7) ≈ 2.807
- f(n) = n² = O(n^(2.807 − ε))
- Case 1 → **T(n) = Θ(n^2.807)** — beats naive O(n³).

**Karatsuba multiplication**: `T(n) = 3 T(n/2) + O(n)`
- a=3, b=2, c = log_2(3) ≈ 1.585
- f(n) = n = O(n^(1.585 − ε))
- Case 1 → **T(n) = Θ(n^1.585)** — beats naive O(n²).

**Divide-and-conquer max**: `T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(1)`
- a=2, b=2, c = 1, f(n) = 1
- f(n) = 1 = O(n^(1 − ε))
- Case 1 → **T(n) = Θ(n)**.

**Limitations of master theorem**:
- Only works for `T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)` form.
- Does NOT work for recurrences like `T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2)` (Fibonacci) or `T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1)`.
- Those need recursion tree or substitution.

sections.title: Recursion Tree Method — Visual and General
sections.content:
When master theorem doesn't apply (or as intuition), **draw the tree** of recursive calls and sum the work per level.

**Merge sort — `T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n)`**:
```
Level 0:     T(n)         → O(n) work
Level 1:   T(n/2) T(n/2)  → 2 · O(n/2) = O(n)
Level 2: T(n/4) ... T(n/4) → 4 · O(n/4) = O(n)
...
Level log(n): T(1) ... T(1) → n · O(1) = O(n)

Total: O(n) per level × log n levels = O(n log n)
```
Same answer as master theorem, but you can *see* it.

**Binary search — `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`**:
```
Level 0: T(n)   → O(1)
Level 1: T(n/2) → O(1)
...
Level log(n): T(1) → O(1)

Total: log n levels × O(1) = O(log n)
```

**Naive Fibonacci — `T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)`**:
```
Level 0:          T(n)
Level 1:    T(n-1)    T(n-2)
Level 2:  T(n-2) T(n-3) T(n-3) T(n-4)
...
```
Each level has ~2x more nodes than the previous. Depth ≈ n.
- Total nodes: 2^n (roughly).
- More precisely: F(n+1) - 1 = O(φ^n) where φ = (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618 (golden ratio).
- **T(n) = O(2^n)** as a loose bound; tighter is Θ(φ^n).

**Why this isn't master-theorem form**: sub-problems don't shrink by the same factor — they shrink by an additive constant. Master theorem requires **multiplicative** shrinkage (n/b).

**Selection sort (recursive)**: `T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)`
- Not master-theorem form.
- Tree: n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 = **O(n²)**.

**T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)** (linear recursion):
- Tree: 1 + 1 + ... + 1 (n times) = **O(n)**.
- Example: linked list traversal, factorial.

sections.title: Converting Exponential to Polynomial — Memoization
Common Recurrences and Their Solutions
sections.content:
Memorize these — they appear constantly:

| Recurrence | Solution | Example |
|---|---|---|
| T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) | O(n) | Linear recursion, factorial |
| T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) | O(n²) | Recursive selection sort |
| T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) | O(log n) | Binary search |
| T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) | O(n) | Divide-by-half linear work |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) | O(n) | Divide and conquer count/max |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) | O(n log n) | Merge sort, quicksort |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n²) | O(n²) | Root dominates |
| T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) | O(n^1.585) | Karatsuba multiplication |
| T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) | O(n²) | Naive matrix multiply |
| T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) | O(n^2.807) | Strassen's algorithm |
| T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) | O(n³) | Naive n×n matrix multiply |
| T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) | O(φ^n) ≈ O(1.618^n) | Naive Fibonacci |
| T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) | O(2^n) | Tower of Hanoi |
| T(n) = T(√n) + O(1) | O(log log n) | Square-root recursion |

**Pattern spotting**:
- **Shrinks by constant (n → n-1)**: usually polynomial or exponential.
- **Shrinks by factor (n → n/b)**: usually polynomial or logarithmic (use master theorem).
- **Multiple sub-problems, same size**: check master theorem cases.
- **Branches into many same-size sub-problems with constant work**: likely n^log_b(a).

sections.title: Space Complexity of Recursion
sections.content:
Don't forget **space**: recursion uses the stack.

**Stack depth = max recursion depth** → O(depth) space.

**Merge sort**:
- Time: O(n log n).
- Space: O(n) for auxiliary arrays + O(log n) stack = **O(n)**.

**Binary search (recursive)**:
- Time: O(log n).
- Space: O(log n) stack.
- Iterative version: O(1) space — usually preferred.

**Naive Fibonacci**:
- Time: O(2^n).
- Space: O(n) stack (depth is n).

**Memoized Fibonacci**:
- Time: O(n).
- Space: O(n) memo + O(n) stack = O(n).

**Tabulated Fibonacci (rolling variables)**:
- Time: O(n).
- Space: O(1).

**Quicksort**:
- Time: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst.
- Space: O(log n) avg stack, O(n) worst (unbalanced partition).
- Java's `Arrays.sort` uses hybrid dual-pivot quicksort; for very large arrays, it also considers stack depth.

**DFS on a graph**:
- Time: O(V + E).
- Space: O(V) stack (if graph is a long path).

**Tail recursion**:
- In languages with tail-call optimization (Scala, Scheme), O(1) space.
- **Java does NOT optimize tail calls** — stack still grows O(depth).
- Convert to a loop manually if stack overflow is a risk.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Write a recurrence T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)** for divide-and-conquer; solve with master theorem.
- **Master theorem** applies to `T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)` form only.
- **Critical exponent**: c = log_b(a).
- **Case 1**: f(n) polynomially smaller than n^c → T(n) = Θ(n^c). Leaves dominate.
- **Case 2**: f(n) = Θ(n^c) → T(n) = Θ(n^c log n). Balanced.
- **Case 3**: f(n) polynomially bigger than n^c → T(n) = Θ(f(n)). Root dominates.
- **Merge sort**: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → Case 2 → O(n log n).
- **Binary search**: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → Case 2 → O(log n).
- **Strassen**: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) → Case 1 → O(n^2.807).
- **Fibonacci**: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) — not master form — recursion tree shows O(φ^n) ≈ O(1.618^n) or loosely O(2^n).
- **Recursion tree** — draw and sum; works for any recurrence, more general than master.
- **Substitution method** — guess and prove by induction.
- **Memoization** converts exponential to polynomial when subproblems overlap.
- **Space = O(max recursion depth)** — don't forget the stack.
- **Java does NOT optimize tail calls** — deep recursion risks StackOverflowError.
- **Common traps**: trying master theorem on non-master recurrences; forgetting the regularity condition in Case 3; confusing log base.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
To analyze a recursive algorithm, write a recurrence that expresses its running time on size n in terms of sub-problems, then solve it.

**Three standard techniques**

**1. Substitution method**
- Guess a bound
- Prove by induction
- Used when you already suspect the answer

**2. Recursion tree**
- Draw the tree of recursive calls
- Compute work at each level
- Sum up
- Intuitive and general — works for most recurrences

**3. Master theorem**
- Plug-and-play formula for `T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)` form
- `a` = number of sub-problems
- `n/b` = size of each sub-problem
- `f(n)` = non-recursive work per call

**Master theorem — three cases**
- Compute c = log_b(a)
- Case 1: f(n) polynomially smaller than n^c → T(n) = Θ(n^c). Leaves dominate.
- Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^c) → T(n) = Θ(n^c log n). Balanced.
- Case 3: f(n) polynomially bigger than n^c → T(n) = Θ(f(n)). Root dominates.

**Classic examples**

**Merge sort**: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
- a=2, b=2, c = log_2(2) = 1
- f(n) = n = Θ(n^1) → Case 2
- T(n) = O(n log n)

**Binary search**: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
- a=1, b=2, c = 0
- f(n) = 1 = Θ(n^0) → Case 2
- T(n) = O(log n)

**Strassen's matrix multiply**: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²)
- a=7, b=2, c ≈ 2.807
- f(n) = n² is polynomially smaller than n^2.807 → Case 1
- T(n) = O(n^2.807) — beats naive O(n³)

**Karatsuba multiplication**: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n)
- a=3, b=2, c ≈ 1.585
- Case 1 → T(n) = O(n^1.585) — beats naive O(n²)

**Naive Fibonacci** — NOT master theorem form
- T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)
- Sub-problems shrink by additive constant, not multiplicative factor
- Use recursion tree: branches into 2 per level, depth n
- T(n) = O(2^n), more tightly O(φ^n) ≈ O(1.618^n)
- Memoization reduces to O(n)
- Matrix exponentiation: O(log n)

**Recursion tree — when master theorem doesn't apply**

Draw the tree:
- Merge sort: log n levels, O(n) work per level → O(n log n)
- Binary search: log n levels, O(1) per level → O(log n)
- Fibonacci: n levels, branches doubling → O(2^n)
- Linear recursion T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1): n levels, O(1) each → O(n)

**Memorize these common recurrences**
- T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) → O(n)
- T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) → O(n²)
- T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)
- T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n)
- T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) → O(n)
- T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n)
- T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) → O(2^n) (Tower of Hanoi)
- T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) → O(φ^n)

**Memoization converts exponential to polynomial**
- Naive Fib: O(2^n) due to overlapping sub-problems
- Memoized Fib: O(n) — each sub-problem computed once
- Tabulated Fib with rolling vars: O(n) time, O(1) space
- This is the heart of dynamic programming

**Space complexity — don't forget the stack**
- Merge sort: O(n) aux + O(log n) stack = O(n)
- Binary search: O(log n) stack
- Naive Fib: O(n) stack
- Quicksort: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst
- Tail recursion: Java does NOT optimize — stack still grows
- For deep recursion, convert to iterative to avoid StackOverflowError

**Common traps**

**1. Applying master theorem to non-master form**
- Fibonacci — use recursion tree
- Tower of Hanoi — use recursion tree

**2. Forgetting the regularity condition in Case 3**
- a·f(n/b) ≤ k·f(n) for some k < 1
- Usually holds for polynomials

**3. Confusing log base**
- log_b(a) — log of a base b
- Don't confuse with log n (which is base 2 by convention in CS)

**4. Forgetting space complexity**
- Recursion always uses O(depth) stack space
- Can cause StackOverflow even if time is fine

**Recommendation:** When given a recursive algorithm, **write the recurrence first** — identify `a` (number of sub-problems), `b` (shrinkage factor), and `f(n)` (non-recursive work). If the form is `T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)`, apply **master theorem** with `c = log_b(a)` and the three cases. If not (like Fibonacci or Tower of Hanoi), use the **recursion tree** — draw the levels, compute work per level, sum up. **Memorize the common recurrences** — merge sort's O(n log n), binary search's O(log n), Fibonacci's O(2^n) — these appear constantly. When you see an **exponential recurrence with overlapping sub-problems**, reach for **memoization** to convert to polynomial — this is the essence of dynamic programming. Always compute **space complexity** too: recursion is O(depth) stack space, and Java does **not** optimize tail calls — deep recursion can StackOverflow. For interviews, practice deriving the recurrence from the code in one pass: read the function, count sub-calls, count non-recursive work, write the recurrence, apply master theorem. The most common mistake is trying to force master theorem onto non-master-form recurrences; when in doubt, **draw the tree**.
